methods.label: List the possible reversed factors
methods.explanation:
The wording does not explicitly require the reversed number to retain two digits. If a leading zero is dropped, reversing \(10\) gives \(01\), whose numerical value is \(1\). We must account for this possibility before claiming a unique product.

Let \(r\) be the numerical value obtained by reversing the digits of \(a\). Then \(rb=161\), and \(1\le r\le99\). Since \(161=7\cdot23\), with both factors prime, its positive factors are \(1,7,23,161\). The factor \(161\) is too large to be \(r\), leaving exactly three cases.

If \(r=1\), then \(a=10\) and \(b=161\), so \(ab=1610\).

If \(r=7\), then \(a=70\) and \(b=23\), so \(ab=1610\).

If \(r=23\), then \(a=32\) and \(b=7\), so \(ab=224\).

These cases exhaust the possible reversed factors. Thus the statement as written permits both \(224\) and \(1610\), so it does not determine a unique product. If we additionally require the reversed number to have two digits, only \(r=23\) remains, giving \(224\), choice \(\mathrm{E}\). This is the only listed possible product.
